sections.heading: Heritage Homes, Aging Tanks
sections.html:
Sackville's wooden housing stock is one of the town's charms, and one of its quiet risks. Many of these homes went up long before oil heat existed, so the tanks were retrofitted decades ago into stone-foundation cellars, crawlspaces, and side yards. Steel tanks rust from the inside out, which means a tank can look fine while corrosion works away underneath, and the damp air that rolls in off the Tantramar marshes doesn't do outdoor tanks any favours either.

Here's what's worth checking on your own tank before the cold sets in:

  • An oil smell in the basement or near the tank
  • Wet spots, weeping seams, or rust blisters on the tank body
  • Rusted or wobbly legs, or a tank settling into soft ground
  • No legible label or age tag anywhere on the tank

If any of that sounds familiar, don't wait for a failure in the middle of a cold snap. A free written estimate now beats an emergency call when the furnace is down and the floor is wet.

sections.heading: The Insurance Letter, and What It Actually Means
sections.html:
The most common call we get from Sackville starts with a letter. Insurers across New Brunswick now ask for the age and condition of oil tanks, and most want them under a set age, often somewhere between 15 and 25 years depending on the company and the tank type. If yours is older than that, or you can't prove its age, they can require a new one before they'll renew the policy.

It's stressful, but it's rarely the emergency it feels like. You usually have time to get a quote, book the work, and send in the paperwork. In most cases we complete the replacement in a single day and hand you dated documentation your insurer can put straight in your file. Most standard above-ground replacements in our area land between $2,500 and $4,500 CAD, and Sackville jobs sit in that same range. Our cost guide breaks down what pushes a job toward either end.

Some Sackville homeowners use the letter as the push to leave oil behind entirely. If that's you, we can do a clean tank removal once your new heating system is in, and document the decommissioning properly.

sections.heading: Serving Sackville, Middle Sackville, and the Border Country
sections.html:
We cover Sackville proper along with Middle Sackville, Upper Sackville, and the rural roads across the Tantramar area, out toward Dorchester, Aulac, and the Nova Scotia border. Sitting right off the Trans-Canada makes Sackville one of the easier stops in our Southeast New Brunswick service area, so scheduling is rarely a problem. We also work in neighbouring Memramcook, and can often book nearby jobs together.

A word to landlords: rental homes near Mount Allison see hard winter use, and a mid-term tank failure means displaced students and a scramble in exam season. If your rental still heats with oil, a look at the tank before September is cheap peace of mind. The same goes if you're buying or selling, since a tank with no proof of age can stall a closing.

And if you're out on the marsh side of town, keep an eye on outdoor tank legs and pads. Ground that stays wet most of the year shifts and settles, and a leaning tank puts stress on lines and fittings. If yours has started to tilt, or you ever smell oil, call the 24/7 emergency line and treat it as urgent.

faq.q: My insurer gave me a deadline to replace the oil tank in my Sackville home. How fast can you move?
faq.a: Usually we can get you a written estimate within a few days, and most residential replacements are finished in a single day once the tank size and access are confirmed. Every job comes with dated paperwork you can send straight to your insurance company. Call as soon as the letter arrives and the deadline won't become a problem.

faq.q: I own a student rental near Mount Allison. Can you work around my tenants?
faq.a: Yes, and it's a smart call. We can schedule around the academic year, and late spring through August is the easiest window since many units sit empty. A tank replaced before September means no mid-winter failure, no displaced tenants, and clean paperwork for your insurer.

faq.q: Could my older Sackville property have a buried oil tank?
faq.a: It's possible, especially on heritage properties that changed heating systems decades ago. Watch for a fill or vent pipe in the yard that doesn't connect to anything obvious, or a patch of ground where grass won't grow. Don't dig on a guess. We can locate the tank, remove it, and document the site for your lawyer and insurer through our buried oil tank removal service.
